summary: A conditional grant of rights to specific Hewlett-Packard patents for use in IETF standards-track network management MIB modules. It is a legal statement, not a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1988 records Hewlett-Packard's conditional promise not to assert claims under certain patents when parties use its search address technology in qualifying IETF network management standards. The promise does not cover proprietary MIB modules and can end under a stated condition.

subtitle: A conditional Hewlett-Packard patent grant for certain standards-track network management modules.

tldr.problem: Hewlett-Packard held patents covering search address technology that the IETF wanted to include in standards-track network management MIB modules.
tldr.mechanism: HP promises not to assert claims under specified patents against parties implementing a qualifying standards-track MIB module for the Internet-standard network management framework.
tldr.outcome: The grant excludes proprietary MIB modules and ends for a party that asserts a patent against HP concerning systems using search address technology.

today: RFC 1988 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC records HP's conditional grant as of August 1996 and does not state what happened to it later.

sections.title: A Legal Notice, Not a Technical Standard
sections.content:
RFC 1988 is an announcement by Hewlett-Packard (HP) about a conditional grant of rights to use patented network management technology with the IETF's Internet-standard network management framework. The memo explicitly says it is not a standard.

The technology is called search address and is described as a method for mapping network devices. HP offered it to help include the technology in IETF standards-track Management Information Base (MIB) modules. The memo says the confirmatory license mentioned in it is optional because the grant is automatic.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC records a company's statement about patent rights, not rules for how a network operates. It concerns one device-mapping technique and certain IETF network management modules.

sections.title: Which Implementations the Grant Covers
sections.content:
HP promises not to assert claims in US Patents 5,293,635 and 5,421,024, their listed continuations and related applications, or their non-US counterparts against a party that makes, uses, sells, imports, or offers an implementation of an IETF standards-track MIB module containing HP's contributed search address technology or a derivative.

The module must be used to implement the Internet-standard network management framework. The grant does not include a right to put the technology into proprietary MIB modules.
sections.plainLanguage: The promise applies only to implementations of qualifying IETF standards-track MIB modules used with the Internet-standard network management framework. It does not cover proprietary MIB modules.

sections.title: When the Grant Ends
sections.content:
The grant permanently terminates for a party, and its subsidiaries, if that party asserts a patent it owns or controls against HP or an HP subsidiary concerning implementation or operation of a system using search address technology. The termination takes effect on the date the patent is asserted.

The memo says a party may request written confirmation of the grant or a license under another HP patent under HP's then-current terms, conditions, and royalty rates.
sections.plainLanguage: If a party asserts its own patent against HP over a system using search address technology, this grant ends for that party and its subsidiaries. The memo also gives a contact for requesting confirmation or another patent license.
